claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings is governed by nanoscale crystalline/amorphous and amorphous/amorphous interfaces.
Nanoscale crystalline/amorphous interfaces suppress shear-banding instability.
Nanoscale amorphous/amorphous interfacial regions suppress localized shear banding.
Nanoscale amorphous/amorphous interfacial regions promote homogeneous deformation by facilitating the nucleation and distribution of many shear transformation zones.
High-density crystalline/amorphous interfaces act as sinks that reduce shear-banding instability.
Introducing ductile crystalline phases into metallic-glass-based composites is a route to crystalline/amorphous interfacial structures.
Developing nanostructured amorphous alloys can introduce amorphous/amorphous interfacial regions.
The proposed high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings contain nanoscale crystalline/amorphous and amorphous/amorphous interfaces.
Suppression of shear-band propagation promotes greater plasticity.
The proposed interfaces improve resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
The proposed interfaces increase tensile strength.
Composition and processing conditions affect the formation and stability of the proposed nanoscale interfaces.
Interface density limits or controls the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism.
The exact mechanism by which these interfaces suppress shear banding and promote homogeneous deformation is not fully understood.
A controlled comparison should test high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings with and without the proposed nanoscale interfaces.
The comparison should measure tensile strength, ductility, shear-banding behavior, and microstructure.
Failure of the interfaces to improve resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation and mechanical properties relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
